title: CRISP: Reading the Sparse-Attention Routing Decision Straight Off the Attention Map
hook: Long-context prefill is quadratic, so servers route attention heads to sparse patterns. CRISP shows the routing decision is already readable off the attention map's structure.
key_points: Prefill self-attention scales quadratically, making it the bottleneck for long-context inference.
Dynamic routers pick a sparse pattern per head at runtime, but pay overhead for indirect proxies like JS divergence.
CRISP replaces JSD routing with C_struct, which measures mass at Vertical-Slash-compatible positions and reproduces the same decisions with no pooled matmul or KL step.
The authors show strictly cumulative coverage thresholds accumulate O(n) background noise at long contexts — the 'post-softmax mass cliff'.
A sink-aware threshold grounded in the noise floor fixes it: up to +28.0 pp on retrieval tasks and up to 5.30x attention speedup at 512k tokens.
content_html: Serving a long prompt means paying for attention that grows quadratically with its length. The standard mitigation is sparse attention, and the current generation of methods routes each attention head to a sparse pattern dynamically, at runtime. Nguyen and colleagues identify two structural problems with that paradigm and fix both in CRISP.
extra_html:
How it works

First, routing: existing methods score a proxy attention map with Jensen-Shannon divergence, which costs a pooled matmul plus a KL computation. The authors show the decision is readable directly from the map's structure, and define C_struct — the attention mass sitting at Vertical-Slash-compatible positions — which reproduces JSD's routing decisions without either cost. Second, budget allocation: they formalize a "post-softmax mass cliff" and argue theoretically that strictly cumulative coverage thresholds accumulate O(n) background noise as context grows. CRISP instead uses a sink-aware threshold anchored to the noise floor.

Why it matters

Across InfiniteBench, RULER, and LongBench on two model families, the authors report CRISP as the strongest sparse method overall, matching or exceeding exact dense attention on retrieval-heavy benchmarks — up to +28.0 percentage points over baselines on retrieval tasks — and up to a 5.30x attention speedup at 512k tokens. The framing worth keeping: in sparse attention, how you decide what to keep is as much a source of error as how much you keep.

related.title: FlashPrefill V2: Block-Sparse Prefill Attention for Long-Context Serving
related.hook: Prefill is where long-context inference burns its compute. This turns a sparse-attention prototype into a production backend — and reports up to 47x over FlashAttention-2 at 128K.

related.title: Multi-Query Attention: Faster Decoding
related.hook: Share one key/value head across all query heads - the KV cache shrinks by a factor of H and decoding gets dramatically faster with barely any quality cost.

prereqs.title: Attention Is All You Need
prereqs.hook: Drop recurrence and convolution, keep only attention — and you get a model that trains in parallel and powers nearly every LLM since.

flashcards.prompt: What does CRISP's C_struct proxy measure, and what does it replace?
flashcards.back_html: It measures attention mass at Vertical-Slash-compatible positions, reproducing JS-divergence routing decisions while eliminating the pooled matmul and the KL divergence computation.

flashcards.prompt: According to CRISP, what goes wrong with a strictly cumulative coverage threshold for selecting attention blocks at long context?

choices.text: It accumulates O(n) background noise, so the selection drifts as context grows
It becomes numerically unstable in bfloat16
It always selects too few blocks, hurting throughput

flashcards.explanation_html: Past the post-softmax mass cliff, the tail is mostly noise; summing to a fixed coverage fraction sweeps in O(n) of it. CRISP uses a sink-aware threshold grounded in the noise floor instead.

flashcards.prompt: Why is prefill, not decode, the target of this line of work?
flashcards.back_html: Prefill attention over the whole prompt scales quadratically with sequence length, so at long context it dominates cost — unlike per-token decode.
